_about: One entry per fact marker [[f:id]]. status "needs_aph_source" means the fact could not be sourced without www.aph.gov.au or ParlInfo.

facts.claim: A bill is a written proposal for a new law or a change to an existing law.

quotes.quote: Laws start as bills – a written proposal for a new law or a change to an existing law.

facts.claim: To become law, a bill must be agreed to in identical form by both houses.

quotes.quote: a bill must be agreed to in identical form by both the Senate and House of Representatives

facts.claim: Royal assent is the Governor-General signing a bill, the final step in making it a law.

quotes.quote: The signing of a bill by the Governor-General, which is the final step in making a bill into a law.

facts.claim: Once signed by the Governor-General, a bill becomes an Act of Parliament.

quotes.quote: After a bill is signed by the Governor-General it becomes an Act of Parliament – a law.

facts.claim: Ideas for laws come from departments, political parties, community and business groups, and committees.

quotes.quote: Ideas for new laws can come from many different places:
A government department may tell its minister about a problem that needs fixing.
Political parties have their own ideas about how Australia should be governed.
They can speak to members of parliament with suggestions for bills.
If the issue requires action, the committee may suggest that a bill be introduced.

facts.claim: Most bills are government bills, introduced by ministers.

quotes.quote: Most bills are introduced by government ministers.

facts.claim: Other members can introduce their own bills, known as private members' or private senators' bills.

quotes.quote: Other members of parliament can introduce their own bills, known as private members' or private senators' bills.

facts.claim: Since 1901, only about 30 private bills have passed.

quotes.quote: Since Federation in 1901, only about 30 private bills have passed the Parliament.

facts.claim: Private bills rarely pass because most time goes to government business and the government usually has a House majority.

quotes.quote: the Senate and House of Representatives spend most of their time considering government business
the government usually has the majority in the House of Representatives, so a private bill will only succeed if the government supports it.

facts.claim: A bill is introduced in the house where the person responsible for it sits.

quotes.quote: A bill – proposed law – is introduced in the house where the person responsible for it sits.

facts.claim: Most ministers are in the House, so most bills start there.

quotes.quote: Most ministers are members of the House, so most bills are introduced there.

facts.claim: Bills that tax or spend public money cannot start in the Senate (Constitution s 53).

quotes.quote: Proposed laws appropriating revenue or moneys, or imposing taxation, shall not originate in the Senate.
money and taxation bills must be introduced in the House of Representatives.

facts.claim: At the first reading the bill is introduced and its title read for the first time.

quotes.quote: in which the bill is introduced and the title of the bill is read for the first time.

facts.claim: The Clerk reads a bill's title 3 times in each house; each reading marks a stage passed.

quotes.quote: To pass through the Senate or House of Representatives, the title of the bill must be read out 3 times by the Clerk.
Each time the Clerk reads the title of the bill it signals the bill has passed a different stage.

facts.claim: OPAX bill pages list each stage recorded for the bill with its date; a stage can appear once per debate day, and the list usually starts with "Introduced".

quotes.quote: Recorded stages
"stage": "introduced"
"stage": "second_reading"

facts.derived: r7076 lists "second_reading" in the House on 6 dates (2023-09-06 to 2023-10-18). Of 2,989 federal bills, 2,985 start with "introduced"; 3 start with "second_reading" and 1 with an exposure draft, so "usually".

facts.claim: The second reading starts with a motion that the bill now be read a second time.

quotes.quote: When a member of parliament says ‘I move that this bill now be read a second time’
the member or senator (usually a minister responsible for the bill) moves a motion – asks – that it be read a second time.

facts.claim: In the second reading debate members discuss the main idea of the bill and say why they support or oppose it.

quotes.quote: members of parliament discuss the principle or main idea of the bill and can explain why they support or oppose the bill.

facts.claim: Passing the second reading vote signals agreement with the main idea; the bill then moves to later stages including amendments.

quotes.quote: If the vote passes, it signals that senators or members agree with the main idea of the bill
The bill can then progress through the next stages, including discussion of amendments – changes – to the bill.

facts.claim: The Federation Chamber is the House's second meeting place; it can sit at the same time as the House and all members may attend.

quotes.quote: The Federation Chamber is the second meeting place of the House of Representatives and can operate at the same time as the House.
All members of the House can attend the Federation Chamber.

facts.claim: The Federation Chamber debates bills on which agreement is expected.

quotes.quote: debating bills on which there is expected to be agreement

facts.claim: Divisions cannot be held in the Federation Chamber.

quotes.quote: although divisions – formal recorded votes – cannot be taken there.

facts.claim: Federation Chamber decisions must be confirmed by the House.

quotes.quote: All decisions made in the Federation Chamber need to be confirmed by the House of Representatives.

facts.claim: Either house can send a bill to a committee.

quotes.quote: Either house of Parliament can send a bill to a committee for detailed examination.

facts.claim: Committees usually have 6 to 10 members.

quotes.quote: They are usually made up of 6 to 10 members of parliament and have a mix of government and non-government members.

facts.claim: Committees invite submissions, then hold hearings.

quotes.quote: Individuals and groups are invited to send submissions – opinions and proposals – to committees.
they invite people or groups to appear at hearings to provide more information or answer questions from committee members.

facts.claim: Committees report to Parliament and may suggest changes to a bill.

quotes.quote: After the hearings are finished, the committee writes a report which is presented to Parliament.
A committee might suggest changes to a bill or make other recommendations for the Houses to consider.

facts.claim: The Senate may refer a bill to a Senate committee for inquiry, even while it is still in the House.

quotes.quote: the Senate may refer the text of the bill to a Senate committee for inquiry (this can happen while the bill is in the House).

facts.claim: Committees investigate issues as well as bills.

quotes.quote: Committees investigate issues and bills in detail.

facts.claim: Members may use a committee report to decide their vote or to draft amendments.

quotes.quote: Members of parliament might use the report to help them decide how they will vote on a bill or to develop bills or amendments

facts.claim: Consideration in detail is an optional stage after the second reading where the bill is discussed in detail.

quotes.quote: Consideration in detail (optional stage) – members discuss the bill in detail, including any changes to the bill

facts.claim: The detailed stage is called consideration in detail in the House and committee of the whole in the Senate.

quotes.quote: A stage in the passage of a bill through the House of Representatives, in which members discuss the bill in detail, including any suggested changes.
A stage in the passage of a bill through the Senate, in which senators discuss the bill in detail, including any suggested changes.

facts.claim: Most amendments are considered at consideration in detail or committee of the whole, where members speak and vote on each.

quotes.quote: Amendments to bills are most often considered during committee of the whole in the Senate or consideration in detail in the House of Representatives.
can speak about each amendment and vote for or against each amendment.

facts.claim: Any member can move an amendment.

quotes.quote: Any member of parliament can suggest an amendment to a bill. This is called 'moving an amendment'.

facts.claim: Amendments are given in writing to the Clerk, who circulates copies.

quotes.quote: An amendment must be submitted in writing to the Clerk of the Senate or House.
The Clerk then distributes copies so that everyone can read the amendment

facts.claim: If a majority agree to an amendment, the bill is changed.

quotes.quote: If the majority agree to an amendment, the bill is changed.

facts.claim: Non-government members move most amendments because most bills are government bills.

quotes.quote: Independent, minor party and opposition members are more likely to suggest amendments. This is because most bills introduced to Parliament are government bills

facts.claim: At the third reading members vote on the bill in its final form; if it passes, that house has passed the bill.

quotes.quote: in which members of parliament vote on the bill in its final form.
3rd reading – members vote on the bill in its final form the bill is passed in the House of Representatives and sent to the Senate.

facts.claim: After the House passes a bill, the Speaker sends a message to the Senate asking it to agree.

quotes.quote: signs a document, known as a ‘message’, addressed to the President of the Senate, requesting the Senate’s ‘concurrence’ – agreement – with the bill.

facts.claim: In the second house a similar series of stages is followed.

quotes.quote: In the Senate a bill goes through the following stages:
it is sent to the other house – in this case, the Senate – where a similar process is followed.

facts.claim: The Senate can debate a bill immediately, send it to a committee, or schedule it for later.

quotes.quote: decide to immediately debate the bill, send it to a committee for closer examination or schedule debate on the bill for a later day.

facts.claim: Amendments made in either house must be agreed to by both.

quotes.quote: Amendments can be introduced in either the Senate or the House of Representatives, and must be agreed to by both.

facts.claim: When the second house changes a bill, the first house must agree to those changes too.

quotes.quote: or passes it with amendments to which the House of Representatives will not agree
Amendments can be introduced in either the Senate or the House of Representatives, and must be agreed to by both.
Consideration of Senate Message - Agree with Senate amendments and so pass bill

facts.claim: If one house does not pass a bill, it cannot become law.

quotes.quote: If one of the houses doesn't pass a bill – a proposal for a new law – then it cannot become a law.

facts.claim: The originating house may pass it again, change it, or lay it aside.

quotes.quote: pass the bill again and send it back to the second house
change the bill so the second house will be more likely to pass it
lay the bill aside (not go forward with the bill).

facts.claim: The double dissolution path in s 57 applies to bills passed by the House of Representatives.

quotes.quote: If the House of Representatives passes any proposed law, and the Senate rejects or fails to pass it

facts.claim: The trigger: the Senate rejects (or fails to pass, or amends unacceptably) a House bill twice, three months apart.

quotes.quote: if after an interval of three months the House of Representatives, in the same or the next session, again passes the proposed law
The Senate again rejects or fails to pass the bill, or passes the same bill with amendments to which the House will not agree.

facts.note: Copy simplifies "rejects, fails to pass, or passes with amendments the House will not agree to" to "blocks".

facts.claim: The Prime Minister can then ask the Governor-General for an election for every seat in both houses.

quotes.quote: the Prime Minister can ask the Governor-General to call an election for all the seats in the House of Representatives and the Senate.

facts.claim: There have been 7 double dissolutions.

quotes.quote: There have been 7 double dissolutions of the Australian Parliament: 1914, 1951, 1974, 1975, 1983, 1987 and 2016.

facts.claim: If the deadlock continues after the election, a joint sitting can be called where senators and members vote together.

quotes.quote: the Governor-General may call a joint sitting of all senators and members of the House of Representatives.
At a joint sitting, all senators and members vote together on the bill or bills.

facts.claim: There has been only one joint sitting, in 1974.

quotes.quote: There has only been one joint sitting of the Australian Parliament.
In 1974, the 6 bills that had triggered a double dissolution were reintroduced into Parliament

facts.claim: The Governor-General can return a bill with suggested amendments (Constitution s 58).

quotes.quote: send the bill back to the Parliament with suggestions for amendments – changes.
The Governor-General may return to the House in which it originated any proposed law so presented to him

facts.claim: No Governor-General has refused royal assent.

quotes.quote: No Governor-General has ever refused to give Royal Assent to a bill

facts.claim: An Act starts on the date it sets, or 28 days after royal assent if none is given.

quotes.quote: starts on the date included in the law or, if no date is given, 28 days after Royal Assent.

facts.claim: OPAX says stage dates do not establish commencement.

quotes.quote: Stage dates describe the parliamentary progress recorded by the source. They do not establish when provisions commence.

facts.claim: A money bill introduces a tax or spends money.

quotes.quote: A proposed law that introduces a tax or suggests spending money for a particular purpose.

facts.claim: The Budget is a set of appropriation bills.

quotes.quote: The Budget is a collection of bills – proposed laws – called appropriation bills.

facts.claim: The Senate cannot amend tax bills or the bill for the ordinary annual services of the Government.

quotes.quote: The Senate may not amend proposed laws imposing taxation, or proposed laws appropriating revenue or moneys for the ordinary annual services of the Government.

facts.note: Constitution s 53 limits Senate amendment to these bills (and to bills increasing a charge or burden); it does not cover every money bill. Copy follows s 53, not the broader PEO wording.

facts.claim: The Senate may return such a bill requesting changes; the House may make them if it sees fit.

quotes.quote: return to the House of Representatives any proposed law which the Senate may not amend, requesting, by message, the omission or amendment
And the House of Representatives may, if it thinks fit, make any of such omissions or amendments

facts.claim: Acts set a framework and can give the power to make detailed rules to a minister or expert body.

quotes.quote: These laws provide a general framework and don’t include details about when, where and how the laws might be applied.
give the power to make decisions about the details of these complex laws to the person or group with expert knowledge

facts.claim: Delegated legislation includes regulations made by ministers or office holders under an Act.

quotes.quote: Rules or regulations made by a government minister, executive office-holder or government department using power that is given to them by the Parliament.
There are different types of delegated law including determinations, regulations, ordinances and orders.

facts.claim: Delegated law has the same power as an Act.

quotes.quote: Delegated law has the same power as a law made by the Australian Parliament.

facts.claim: It can be made or changed without being debated and passed by Parliament.

quotes.quote: It can be made and changed without having to be debated and passed by the Parliament.

facts.claim: Delegated law must go on a public register, and must be presented to Parliament within 6 sitting days.

quotes.quote: Each delegated law must be listed on a public register.
Then it must be presented to Parliament within 6 sitting days.

facts.claim: Unless it says otherwise, a legislative instrument starts at the start of the day after it is registered (Legislation Act 2003 s 12).

quotes.quote: A legislative instrument or a notifiable instrument commences:
at the start of the day after the day the instrument is registered; or

facts.note: PEO says delegated law "becomes law on the day it is registered"; s 12 sets the default as the next day. Copy follows s 12.

facts.claim: A sitting is a meeting of a house of parliament.

quotes.quote: A meeting of a house of parliament.

facts.claim: The Clerk is the top parliamentary officer of each house.

quotes.quote: The top-level parliamentary officer in the Senate or the House of Representatives.

facts.claim: Prorogation formally closes a session of Parliament before an election.

quotes.quote: A special proclamation to formally close a session of the Parliament, used before a dissolution of the House of Representatives

facts.claim: Within 15 sitting days a member can move to overrule it; the house then has 15 sitting days; with no decision it is overruled.

quotes.quote: Within 15 sitting days, a member of parliament must request the Senate or House of Representatives overrule the delegated law.
The Senate or House of Representatives have 15 sitting days to discuss the delegated law and make a decision.
If there is no discussion or no decision is made, the delegated law is overruled.

facts.claim: Some delegated law cannot be overruled.

quotes.quote: Some delegated law cannot be overruled.

facts.claim: When Parliament is prorogued for an election, bills expire and can be reintroduced in the next Parliament.

quotes.quote: When Parliament is prorogued so a federal election can be held, bills – proposed laws – and other business
Bills and other business can be reintroduced in the next Parliament.

facts.claim: OPAX shows each bill's status from Parliament's bill records, such as lapsed; none of the 1,076 lapsed bills has a royal assent date or an Act.

quotes.quote: Bills, their dates and their divisions come from the parliamentary record
"status": "lapsed"

facts.derived: 1,076 bills in portal/public/bills/au-federal-*.json have status "lapsed"; none has a royal_assent stage or an entry in acts.
facts.note: Reworded rather than defined: PEO never uses "lapse", and the export's parliament field is too unreliable to show each lapse falls at a prorogation.

facts.claim: Most bills take 2 to 3 months; some take years.

quotes.quote: It can take months or even years for a bill to become law but most bills take 2 to 3 months.

facts.claim: Around 200 bills are introduced each year.

quotes.quote: Around 200 bills are introduced into Parliament each year

facts.claim: Parliament is the Monarch (represented by the Governor-General), the Senate and the House of Representatives.

quotes.quote: the Parliament is made up of the Monarch, represented by the Governor-General, and two houses of Parliament: the Senate and the House of Representatives.

facts.claim: Making laws is one of Parliament's main roles.

quotes.quote: One of the main roles of the Australian Parliament is to make laws for the people of Australia.

facts.claim: The House of Representatives has 150 members, and will still have 150 at the next election.

quotes.quote: There are 150 members. Each represents a different electorate.
As at 28 May 2026
the number of seats in the House of Representatives will remain unchanged – at 150 – for Australia’s next federal election.
the total number of House of Representatives seats for each state and territory will remain unchanged
MPs will continue to represent their existing electorates until a federal election is called.

facts.note: AEC entitlement determination of 23 Jul 2026 keeps 150 and every state's count. The SA, Tasmania and ACT redistributions determined on 8 Oct 2026 redraw boundaries within those counts; MPs keep their existing electorates until the election.

facts.claim: An electorate is the area a member represents, also called a seat.

quotes.quote: A geographical area represented by a member of parliament, also referred to as a seat.

facts.claim: Within each state or territory, electorates have about the same number of voters.

quotes.quote: projected enrolment in each electorate should not vary from the projected state or territory average by more than 3.5 per cent.
there is approximately the same number of voters living in each electorate.

facts.note: PEO says "approximately the same" without the state qualifier; the AEC rule is per state or territory, which the copy follows.

facts.claim: A person elected to the House is a member, or MP.

quotes.quote: A person elected to the House of Representatives, also referred to as an MP.

facts.claim: House members are elected at least every 3 years.

quotes.quote: Members are elected to the House of Representatives at least every 3 years.

facts.claim: There are 76 senators: 12 per state and 2 each for the NT and ACT.

quotes.quote: There are 76 senators. Each state is represented by 12 senators, and the Northern Territory and Australian Capital Territory are represented by 2 senators each.
As at 15 May 2026

facts.claim: A senator represents a state or territory.

quotes.quote: A senator is someone who has been elected to represent their state or territory in the Senate.

facts.claim: State senators serve 6 years with half elected every 3 years; territory senators serve 3 years.

quotes.quote: State senators are elected for a period of 6 years
every 3 years half of the state senators are up for re-election
Senators representing the Australian Capital Territory and the Northern Territory have 3-year terms

facts.claim: The Constitution says the House is to be, as nearly as practicable, twice the size of the Senate (s 24).

quotes.quote: the number of such members shall be, as nearly as practicable, twice the number of the senators.

facts.claim: House seats are shared among states in proportion to population (s 24).

quotes.quote: The number of members chosen in the several States shall be in proportion to the respective numbers of their people

facts.claim: Electorate boundaries are redrawn from time to time; projected enrolment should stay within 3.5% of the state or territory average.

quotes.quote: the last redistribution for that state or territory was determined seven years ago
projected enrolment in each electorate should not vary from the projected state or territory average by more than 3.5 per cent.

facts.claim: As at 28 May 2026: government 94, opposition 41, minor parties and independents 15 (1+1+1+2+10).

quotes.quote: Government – 94 members
Opposition – 41 members
Australian Greens – 1 member
Centre Alliance – 1 member
Katter's Australian Party – 1 member
One Nation – 2 members
Independents – 10 members
As at 28 May 2026

facts.claim: As at 15 May 2026: government 30, opposition 27, minor parties and independents 19 (10+4+1+1+1+2).

quotes.quote: Government – 30 senators
Opposition – 27 senators
Australian Greens – 10 senators
One Nation – 4 senators
Jacqui Lambie Network – 1 senator
United Australia Party – 1 senator
Australia's Voice – 1 senator
Independents – 2 senators
As at 15 May 2026

facts.claim: The government is the party or coalition with majority support in the House.

quotes.quote: the party, or coalition of parties, with the support of the majority of members in the House of Representatives.

facts.claim: A coalition is an agreement between parties to form a bigger group.

quotes.quote: An agreement between two or more parliamentary parties to create a bigger group and strengthen their position.

facts.claim: The government may or may not hold a Senate majority.

quotes.quote: The government may or may not hold the majority of seats in the Senate.

facts.claim: A government majority in the Senate is unusual.

quotes.quote: A government majority in the Senate is unusual, so the government must negotiate with senators from the opposition and crossbench.

facts.claim: The Prime Minister leads the government.

quotes.quote: The Prime Minister of Australia is the leader of the Australian Government.

facts.claim: Australians do not vote for the PM; the governing party chooses its leader.

quotes.quote: The people of Australia do not vote for the Prime Minister.
the Prime Minister is chosen by a vote of the members of the party in government.

facts.claim: By convention the PM is a member of the House.

quotes.quote: By convention – tradition – the Prime Minister is always a member of the House of Representatives, not a senator.

facts.claim: The PM is not mentioned in the Constitution.

quotes.quote: The role of Prime Minister is not mentioned in the Australian Constitution.

facts.claim: The PM selects ministers.

quotes.quote: selecting members of the government to be ministers
The Prime Minister chooses experienced and knowledgeable government members to be ministers

facts.claim: A minister's area of responsibility, such as health or defence, is a portfolio.

quotes.quote: Ministers are members of the Australian Government who have been given an area of responsibility for how Australia is run.
This area of responsibility is known as a portfolio. Examples of ministerial portfolios include: health environment transport defence

facts.claim: There are usually about 20 ministers in the House and 10 in the Senate.

quotes.quote: There are usually about 20 ministers in the House of Representatives and 10 in the Senate.

facts.claim: A minister must be or become a senator or member within 3 months (s 64).

quotes.quote: shall hold office for a longer period than three months unless he is or becomes a senator or a member of the House of Representatives.

facts.claim: Cabinet is the PM and about 20 senior ministers.

quotes.quote: It includes the Prime Minister and about 20 ministers who are part of the executive government.

facts.claim: Cabinet meets regularly, often weekly, to decide policy and national issues.

quotes.quote: Cabinet meets on a regular basis, often weekly.
Cabinet's role is to develop government policy and make decisions about national issues.

facts.claim: Cabinet ministers publicly support Cabinet decisions.

quotes.quote: Once Cabinet has made a decision, all Cabinet ministers are expected to support the decision publicly.

facts.claim: The opposition is the largest party or coalition not in government.

quotes.quote: The opposition is the largest party – or coalition of parties – that does not have the support of the majority of members

facts.claim: The opposition is called the alternative government.

quotes.quote: The opposition is sometimes called the alternative government because it could form government if it was to win the support of the majority of members.

facts.claim: The opposition keeps the government accountable and offers alternative policies.

quotes.quote: The opposition has an important role in keeping the government accountable to the Australian Parliament.
providing alternatives to government policies.

facts.claim: The Leader of the Opposition chooses shadow ministers, each following a minister.

quotes.quote: They are chosen by the Leader of the Opposition. Each shadow minister concentrates on the work of a particular minister and government department.
They also act as the opposition spokesperson for the area they are assigned.

facts.claim: Crossbenchers belong to minor parties or are independents with no party.

quotes.quote: An independent is a member of the Australian Parliament who does not belong to a political party.
does not have enough members in the House of Representatives to be the government or the opposition.

facts.claim: Minor parties and independents sit on the crossbench.

quotes.quote: The seats in the Senate or the House of Representatives occupied by minor parties and/or independents.

facts.claim: Without a government Senate majority, crossbench senators can hold the balance of power.

quotes.quote: The government often does not have a majority in the Senate.
Independent and minor party senators can have the balance of power – their vote can decide if a bill is passed or fails.

facts.claim: The Speaker runs the House and the President runs the Senate.

quotes.quote: In the Senate called the President and in the House of Representatives called the Speaker.

facts.claim: Presiding officers call speakers, keep order and conduct votes.

quotes.quote: call on members when it is their turn to speak
conduct votes in the House and announce the results
maintain order and issue warnings if senators have broken the rules

facts.claim: House members vote for the Speaker after an election; senators elect the President.

quotes.quote: After a federal election, members of the House of Representatives vote to choose the Speaker.
They are elected by fellow senators to run the meetings of the Senate.

facts.claim: A whip is chosen by their party to keep it organised and working as a team.

quotes.quote: A party whip is a member of Parliament chosen by their political party to help keep their party organised
They help the party work as a team.

facts.claim: Smaller parties may not have a whip.

quotes.quote: Smaller parties may only have a whip where they have members or choose not to have a whip.

facts.claim: Whips organise attendance and votes, count votes in divisions and negotiate pairs.

quotes.quote: organising party members to make sure they attend and vote together during divisions
counting and recording the votes in a division
so numbers between the government and opposition stay balanced if members are away.

facts.claim: Major parties usually have a chief whip and 2 deputies.

quotes.quote: major parties usually have a chief whip and 2 deputy whips.

facts.claim: The Governor-General represents the King.

quotes.quote: The Governor-General is the King’s representative in Australia.

facts.claim: The King appoints the Governor-General on the PM's recommendation.

quotes.quote: The Governor-General is appointed by the King on the recommendation of the Prime Minister.

facts.claim: By convention the Governor-General follows the government's advice.

quotes.quote: It is an established convention that the Governor-General follows the advice of the Government

facts.claim: Giving royal assent to bills is one of the Governor-General's key jobs.

quotes.quote: One of their most important jobs is giving Royal Assent to bills – proposed laws – passed by the Senate and House of Representatives.

facts.claim: The AEC runs national elections.

quotes.quote: The organisation responsible for running national elections and referendums.

facts.claim: The AEC calls electorates "electoral divisions".

quotes.quote: Find my electoral division
Current federal electoral divisions

facts.claim: A division is a formal recorded vote.

quotes.quote: A division is a formal recorded vote where members of Parliament divide into 2 groups to vote for or against a proposal.

facts.claim: Parliament decides by majority vote.

quotes.quote: The Australian Parliament makes decisions on proposed laws and other issues by a majority vote.

facts.claim: Most decisions are made on the voices.

quotes.quote: Most decisions of the Parliament are made by voting ‘on the voices’.

facts.claim: On the voices, the presiding officer asks for 'aye' or 'no', judges which has more support and announces it.

quotes.quote: asks members of parliament to cast their vote for or against the bill by saying 'aye' or 'no'.
The President or Speaker decides which response has more support and announces the result.

facts.claim: 'Aye' means yes.

quotes.quote: The expression used in Parliament to indicate a 'yes' vote.

facts.claim: A division is held if more than one member challenges the voices result.

quotes.quote: If the result is challenged by more than one member of parliament, a division is held.

facts.claim: Bells ring usually for 4 minutes; then doors lock and latecomers cannot enter.

quotes.quote: The division bells usually ring for 4 minutes.
Once the bells have stopped, the doors are locked.
Members of parliament who arrive after the bells stop are not allowed to enter.

facts.claim: Ayes move to the right of the chair and noes to the left.

quotes.quote: asks those who want to vote for the proposal to move to the right side of their chair
and those voting against to move to the left.

facts.claim: Votes are counted, names recorded and the result announced.

quotes.quote: Votes are counted and the names of those voting are recorded.
The result is announced by the Presiding Officer.

facts.claim: At least 19 senators must vote in a Senate division; 30 members must be present in the House.

quotes.quote: In the Senate, at least 19 senators (one quarter of the total number of senators) must vote in a division for it to count.
In the House, 30 members must be present (one fifth of the total number of members).

facts.claim: The Speaker votes only to break a tie (s 40).

quotes.quote: The Speaker shall not vote unless the numbers are equal, and then he shall have a casting vote.
the Speaker of the House does not vote unless the result is a tie.

facts.claim: The President of the Senate can always vote, keeping state representation equal (s 23).

quotes.quote: The President of the Senate may always vote along with other senators.
This ensures all the states have equal representation when votes are taken in the Senate.

facts.claim: A tied Senate vote fails (s 23).

quotes.quote: when the votes are equal the question shall pass in the negative.
If there is a tied vote in the Senate, the question is not agreed to

facts.claim: Each division has its own OPAX page at /doc/division-...

quotes.quote: `/doc/${String(value).startsWith('division-') ? value : `division-${value}`}`

facts.claim: A division page shows the result, ayes and noes, house and date, the question, party splits and member names.

quotes.quote: esc(`${ayes.toLocaleString()} ayes, ${noes.toLocaleString()} noes`),
id="division-split-head">How the parties voted
id="division-members-head">Who voted which way
